question: In experiments with large language models, which method had the best performance?
answer:
Among the generative AI approaches tested with large language models, **few-shot prompting combined with chain-of-thought prompting** achieved the highest performance, resulting in an F1-score of 0.558.

However, the context notes that even this best-performing generative AI approach was outperformed by all machine learning-based classifiers that used manually annotated training data (the classifier based on BiomedBERT-Large-Abstract, for example, achieved an F1-score of 0.776).

sources.quote: We also fine-tuned the Llama-3-8B [25] large language model (LLM), using 10 epochs and a learning rate of 5e-5.

sources.quote: Based on the 4429 sentences in the held-out test set, zero-shot prompting of an LLM (Llama-3-70B [25]) achieved an F1-score of 0.482 (Table 4).

sources.quote: To address the class imbalance, we performed an additional experiment with the BERT-based classifier in which we under-sampled the "negative" (i.e., majority) class in the training set by removing sentences that were not similar to any of the sentences in the "positive" (i.e., the minority) class.

sources.quote: Based on the 4429 sentences in the held-out test set, fine-tuned models that were pre-trained on corpora in biomedical domains (BioBERT [20], BiomedBERT-Large-Abstract [21], and BiomedBERT-Base-Abstract-Fulltext [22]) or, more specifically, COVID-19 domains (COVID-SciBERT [23] and COVID-Twitter-BERT [24]) outperformed those that were pre-trained on corpora in general domains (DistilBERT-Base [18], BERT-Base [15], and RoBERTa-Large [19]) for detecting sentences that reported patient metadata associated with SARS-CoV-2 sequences, including the Llama-3-8B [25] LLM (Table 2).
